source.title: 12. Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source.citation: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes. 12. Retinopathy, neuropathy, and foot care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care 2026;49(Suppl. 1):S261–S276.

atoms.canonical_statement: Implement strategies that help people with diabetes reach glycemic goals to reduce the risk or slow progression of diabetic retinopathy.
Implement strategies that help people with diabetes reach blood pressure and lipid goals to reduce the risk or slow progression of diabetic retinopathy.
Adults with type 1 diabetes should have an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist 5 years after diabetes onset.
People with type 2 diabetes should have an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at diabetes diagnosis.

After one or more annual eye examinations show no retinopathy and glycemic indicators are within goal, screening every 1–2 years may be considered; any retinopathy warrants at least annual dilated retinal examination, with more frequent ophthalmologist examinations for progressing or sight-threatening disease.

Retinal photography with remote reading or FDA-approved artificial intelligence algorithms is an appropriate diabetic retinopathy screening strategy when the program provides a pathway for timely comprehensive eye-examination referral when indicated.
Counsel people of childbearing potential with preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes who are planning pregnancy or are pregnant about the risk of development or progression of diabetic retinopathy.

People with preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes should receive an eye examination before pregnancy and in the first trimester and may need monitoring every trimester and for 1 year postpartum according to retinopathy severity.

Promptly refer any diabetic macular edema, moderate or worse nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, or any proliferative diabetic retinopathy to an ophthalmologist experienced in diabetic retinopathy management.
Panretinal laser photocoagulation is indicated to reduce vision-loss risk in high-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy and in some cases of severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are a reasonable alternative to traditional panretinal laser photocoagulation for some people with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and reduce vision-loss risk.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are first-line treatment for most eyes with center-involved diabetic macular edema that impairs visual acuity.

Macular focal/grid photocoagulation and intravitreal corticosteroids are reasonable for persistent diabetic macular edema after anti-VEGF therapy or when the eye is not a candidate for anti-VEGF first-line therapy.
Diabetic retinopathy is not a contraindication to aspirin used for cardioprotection because aspirin does not increase retinal hemorrhage risk.

People with diabetes-related vision loss should be counseled about vision rehabilitation and provided or referred for a comprehensive visual-impairment evaluation by a practitioner experienced in vision rehabilitation.
People with diabetes-related vision loss should receive eye-care educational materials and resources in addition to diabetes self-management education.
Assess all people with diabetes for diabetic peripheral neuropathy starting at type 2 diabetes diagnosis or 5 years after type 1 diabetes diagnosis and at least annually thereafter.

Assess distal symmetric polyneuropathy using history plus small-fiber testing with temperature or pinprick and large-fiber testing with vibration using a 128-Hz tuning fork; perform annual 10-g monofilament testing to identify feet at risk for ulceration and amputation.

Assess symptoms and signs of autonomic neuropathy starting at type 2 diabetes diagnosis or 5 years after type 1 diabetes diagnosis, at least annually and when other microvascular complications are present, especially kidney disease and diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

Optimize glucose management to prevent or delay neuropathy in type 1 diabetes and slow neuropathy progression in type 2 diabetes; optimize weight, blood pressure, and lipid management to reduce risk or slow progression of diabetic neuropathy.
Assess and treat painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy and symptoms of autonomic neuropathy to improve quality of life.

Use gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, or sodium channel blockers as initial pharmacologic treatments for diabetic neuropathic pain; combination therapy can provide additional relief, while opioids including tramadol and tapentadol should generally not be used except in rare circumstances.
Perform a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually to identify risk factors for foot ulcers and amputations.

The foot examination should include skin inspection, assessment of deformity, neurologic assessment with 10-g monofilament or Ipswich touch plus at least one additional sensory assessment, and vascular assessment including leg and foot pulses.
People with sensory loss or prior ulceration or amputation should have their feet inspected at every visit.
Obtain history of prior ulceration, amputation, Charcot foot, angioplasty or vascular surgery, cigarette smoking, retinopathy, and renal disease and assess current neuropathy and vascular symptoms.

Initial PAD screening should assess lower-extremity pulses, capillary refill, dependent rubor, elevation pallor, and venous filling; people with suggestive symptoms or decreased/absent pedal pulses should be referred for ankle-brachial index with toe pressures and further vascular assessment.
Use an interprofessional approach facilitated by a podiatrist with appropriate team members for foot ulcers and high-risk feet, including dialysis, Charcot foot, prior ulcer or amputation, and PAD.

Refer smokers with prior lower-extremity complications, loss of protective sensation, structural abnormalities, or PAD to foot-care specialists for preventive care and lifelong surveillance, and provide smoking-cessation information and counseling referral.

Provide preventive foot self-care education to all people with diabetes, including those with loss of protective sensation, with instruction on daily foot surveillance by palpation or visual inspection using an unbreakable mirror.

Recommend specialized therapeutic footwear for people at high ulceration risk, including those with loss of protective sensation, deformity, ulcers, callus formation, poor peripheral circulation, or previous amputation.

For chronic diabetic foot ulcers that fail to heal with optimal standard care alone, consider adjunctive randomized-trial-proven advanced therapies such as negative-pressure wound therapy, selected skin substitutes, or topical oxygen therapy.
Chronic hyperglycemia is the best-established concomitant risk factor for microvascular complications, and optimizing glycemia can prevent or delay microvascular disease in diabetes.
The guideline describes metabolic memory: early near-normal glycemia can produce long-lasting microvascular benefit even after later glycemic levels converge or rise.

Diabetic retinopathy is a neurovascular complication whose prevalence is strongly related to diabetes duration and chronic hyperglycemia; associated risk factors include nephropathy, hypertension, and dyslipidemia.

Evidence on GLP-1 receptor agonists and eye outcomes is conflicting; randomized trials have shown mildly worsening diabetic retinopathy with some agents, while observational studies suggest both possible harms and ocular benefits, and longer purpose-designed studies are needed.

Retinopathy status should be assessed when glucose-lowering therapy is intensified, particularly when rapid A1C reduction is expected, because rapid glycemic improvement can initially worsen retinopathy.

Screening intervals should be individualized to retinopathy status and risk factors; progressing disease, poor glycemic control, advanced retinopathy, or diabetic macular edema warrants more frequent ophthalmic examinations.

Retinal photography with remote interpretation can expand screening access, but ungradable images and abnormal findings require in-person examination, and photography does not replace a comprehensive dilated eye examination.

The chapter names three FDA-authorized autonomous or AI-assisted diabetic retinopathy screening platforms—AEYE-DS, EyeArt, and LumineticsCore—and notes that prospective multicenter diagnostic-accuracy studies exist, while optimal utilization and downstream benefit remain incompletely determined.

Gestational diabetes alone does not require pregnancy eye examinations because it is not associated with increased diabetic retinopathy risk during pregnancy; the pregnancy-specific surveillance recommendations apply to preexisting type 1 or type 2 diabetes.

Pregnancy can aggravate retinopathy in preexisting diabetes, particularly with suboptimal preconception glycemia or advanced retinopathy; rapid intensive glycemic improvement can also produce early worsening, necessitating close follow-up.
Anti-VEGF use during pregnancy should be reserved for clearly indicated situations in which anticipated benefit outweighs potential fetal risk.
Panretinal photocoagulation remains a standard treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, supported by the DRS and ETDRS trials.

For proliferative diabetic retinopathy, intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy can achieve noninferior or superior visual-acuity outcomes relative to panretinal laser over 2 years and may reduce peripheral visual-field loss, vitrectomy, and development of diabetic macular edema.

Anti-VEGF treatment for proliferative diabetic retinopathy generally requires more visits and treatments than panretinal laser; lapses in follow-up are associated with worse visual and anatomic outcomes.

Anti-VEGF treatment of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy reduces later neovascularization and diabetic macular edema but has not improved visual outcomes over 2 years, limiting adoption for this indication.
For center-involved diabetic macular edema, well-designed trials show intravitreal anti-VEGF agents are more effective than laser monotherapy.
In comparative effectiveness data for diabetic macular edema with visual acuity of 20/50 or worse, aflibercept produced better visual outcomes than bevacizumab.
Faricimab and aflibercept 8 mg can achieve visual and anatomic gains similar to aflibercept 2 mg with adjustable dosing intervals up to every 16 weeks.

For eyes with diabetic macular edema but good vision (20/25 or better), close monitoring with anti-VEGF initiation only if vision worsens produced 2-year visual outcomes similar to immediate anti-VEGF initiation.

Lowering blood pressure reduces retinopathy progression, but a systolic target below 120 mmHg did not provide additional retinopathy benefit; fenofibrate may slow progression in dyslipidemia and statins are associated with reduced sight-threatening retinopathy, while thiazolidinedione effects on DME are conflicting.

Vision impairment can interfere with diabetes self-management and daily function and can contribute to depression, anxiety, social isolation, and difficulties at home, work, or school; vision rehabilitation aims to maximize function, independence, and quality of life.
Approximately 12% of U.S. adults with diabetes have some degree of vision impairment.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: In the U.S., ∼12% of adults with diabetes have some level of vision impairment.

atoms.canonical_statement: Diabetic neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion; potentially treatable nondiabetic neuropathies can coexist with diabetes and should be considered.

Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy can exacerbate cardiovascular disease and contribute to heart failure and sudden cardiac death; recognition and treatment of autonomic neuropathy can improve symptoms and quality of life.

DPN assessment should cover small-fiber function with pinprick and temperature, large-fiber function with reflexes, vibration and proprioception, and protective sensation with a 10-g monofilament or Ipswich touch test.

Alternative causes of neuropathy described in the chapter include alcohol and other toxins, neurotoxic medications, vitamin B12 deficiency particularly with chronic metformin use, other nutritional deficiencies, hypothyroidism, kidney disease, malignancy, infections, inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy, inherited neuropathies, and vasculitis.

Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can manifest as resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, bowel dysfunction, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, and altered sweating; targeted testing depends on the involved organ system.

Gastroparesis is a diagnosis of exclusion; after reversible medication effects and mechanical causes are excluded, gastric-emptying scintigraphy of digestible solids over 4 hours is the diagnostic gold standard, with a 13C octanoic acid breath test as an approved alternative.

Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause erectile dysfunction, female sexual dysfunction, and lower urinary tract symptoms; bladder-function evaluation is indicated for recurrent urinary infections, pyelonephritis, incontinence, or a palpable bladder.

No specific treatment currently reverses the underlying nerve damage of diabetic neuropathy; optimal glycemic management can prevent DPN and CAN in type 1 diabetes and may modestly slow progression in type 2 diabetes but does not reverse neuronal loss.

The Look AHEAD randomized lifestyle intervention improved neuropathy symptoms but not neuropathy examination scores; metabolic-surgery evidence is observational, and randomized trials of surgery for neuropathy outcomes are lacking.
Evidence for weight-loss medications and neuropathy is conflicting, and clinical evidence for GLP-1 receptor agonist benefit in DPN remains limited and controversial.

Although dyslipidemia is associated with neuropathy, the optimal lipid intervention for DPN has not been established, and conventional lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy has not shown clear efficacy for treating or preventing DPN.

AAN guidance places gabapentinoids, SNRIs, sodium channel blockers, and tricyclic antidepressants among initial options for painful DPN; head-to-head evidence suggests similar efficacy across major classes and supports combination therapy after inadequate monotherapy response.

Long-term efficacy evidence for opioids in neuropathic pain is lacking, while reviews document harms including abuse, addiction, fractures, myocardial infarction, motor-vehicle crashes, overdose, and mortality; the chapter therefore supports avoiding opioids for painful DPN except rarely.

Capsaicin 8% patch is FDA approved for painful DPN and has high-quality supporting evidence; lidocaine 5% patches have limited supporting data and are more suited to localized rather than widespread pain.

For orthostatic hypotension from autonomic neuropathy, treatment should target symptom reduction rather than normotension, with nonpharmacologic measures and volume repletion first; midodrine and droxidopa are FDA approved when pharmacologic therapy is required.

Gastroparesis management includes a small-particle diet and removal of medications that impair gastrointestinal motility when feasible; metoclopramide is the only FDA-approved drug, but evidence is weak and treatment beyond 12 weeks is no longer recommended because of serious adverse effects.

Domperidone is available outside the United States and erythromycin is useful only short term because of tachyphylaxis; gastric electrical stimulation has very limited DPN data and the chapter states current results do not support it as an effective diabetic gastroparesis therapy.
Erectile-dysfunction treatments may improve quality of life but do not alter the underlying neuropathic pathology or natural history.
Up to 50% of diabetic peripheral neuropathy cases may be asymptomatic.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Up to 50% of diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) cases may be asymptomatic.

atoms.canonical_statement: Risk factors associated with the at-risk diabetic foot include chronic hyperglycemia, peripheral neuropathy or loss of protective sensation, PAD, foot deformities, preulcerative corns or calluses, prior ulcer or amputation, smoking, retinopathy, nephropathy especially dialysis or transplant, and social determinants affecting access to care.

Loss of protective sensation should not be diagnosed with a 10-g monofilament alone; absent monofilament sensation plus another abnormal neurologic test confirms LOPS, and monofilament alone can miss earlier disease.
Toe systolic pressure is more reliable than ankle-brachial index when diabetes causes noncompressible vessels; a toe pressure below 30 mmHg suggests PAD and impaired foot-ulcer healing capacity.
The WIfI staging system is increasingly used to stage PAD severity and amputation risk and to predict diabetic foot-ulcer healing.

Foot-care education improves knowledge and self-care information but has not consistently improved diabetes-care behaviors or achievement of health goals, and knowledge may be rapidly forgotten without reinforcement.

Therapeutic footwear and custom orthoses can reduce peak plantar pressure, but one systematic review found no significant reduction in ulcer incidence at 18 months compared with standard insoles/extradepth shoes and found no evidence for prevention of first ulcers.

A warm, swollen, red foot with or without trauma and without an open ulcer requires evaluation for Charcot neuroarthropathy, foot/ankle radiographs, total non-weight-bearing, and urgent referral to a foot-care specialist.

GLP-1 receptor agonists may reduce lower-extremity amputations, diabetic foot ulcers, and all-cause mortality relative to SGLT2 inhibitors in people with diabetes and PAD, although this evidence is presented as emerging rather than definitive.

In STRIDE, injectable semaglutide in type 2 diabetes with symptomatic PAD improved minimal and pain-free walking distance, quality of life, and a 52-week composite of disease progression, rescue therapy, death, or major adverse limb events.

Canagliflozin was associated with increased lower-limb amputation risk in CANVAS; the mechanism is unknown, and the chapter advises considering temporary discontinuation when a significant lower-limb complication such as DFU, osteomyelitis, or gangrene develops.

Diabetes-related foot infection can threaten the limb and requires prompt diagnosis and treatment; clinically infected ulcers or suspected osteomyelitis warrant appropriate cultures and imaging, abscesses require drainage, and necrotizing infection or wet gangrene requires emergency surgical referral.

The chapter identifies five foundational DFU-treatment principles: pressure offloading, debridement of nonviable tissue, revascularization when needed, management of soft-tissue or bone infection, and wound-appropriate topical dressings.

If a diabetic foot ulcer fails to shrink by at least 50% after 4 weeks of appropriate wound management, advanced wound therapy should be considered after deformity and osteomyelitis have been addressed.

Advanced-wound-therapy evidence is difficult to generate because wound-healing trials are heterogeneous, often exclude chronic kidney disease or dialysis populations, and frequently cannot blind participants or clinicians; systematic reviews and observational data therefore supplement RCT evidence.

Hyperbaric oxygen has one positive randomized trial but other higher-quality studies have not corroborated broad benefit; the chapter does not support widespread use for nonhealing DFU in the absence of ischemia or infection.

Several high-quality randomized trials and systematic reviews/meta-analyses support topical oxygen therapy for healing chronic diabetic foot ulcers at 12 weeks, with home-based delivery, high participation, and few reported adverse events.

When adjunctive advanced wound therapy is required, products or modalities supported by robust randomized trials or systematic reviews and grade A evidence should generally be preferred over options with weaker evidence.
In a multicenter trial of people with diabetes and foot ulceration, peripheral neuropathy was a component cause in 78% of participants.

population.label: People with diabetes and foot ulceration in a multicenter trial

concept.text: Peripheral neuropathy as a component cause of foot ulceration

atoms.canonical_statement: IWGDF risk category 0 (Very low): No LOPS and no PAD; suggested foot examination frequency is Annually.
IWGDF risk category 1 (Low): LOPS or PAD; suggested foot examination frequency is Every 6–12 months.
IWGDF risk category 2 (Moderate): LOPS + PAD, LOPS + foot deformity, or PAD + foot deformity; suggested foot examination frequency is Every 3–6 months.
IWGDF risk category 3 (High): LOPS or PAD plus history of foot ulcer, amputation, or kidney failure; suggested foot examination frequency is Every 1–3 months.
